title: I. Kolya Krassotkin
paragraphs: It was the beginning of November. A hard frost had set in—eleven degrees Réaumur, without snow—but a little dry snow had fallen on the frozen ground during the night, and a sharp, dry wind was lifting and blowing it along the dreary streets of our town, especially around the market-place. It was a dull morning, but the snow had stopped.

Not far from the market-place, close to Plotnikov's shop, there stood a small house, very clean both outside and in. It belonged to Madame Krassotkin, the widow of a former provincial secretary who had been dead for fourteen years. His widow, still a pleasant-looking woman of thirty-two, was living in her neat little house on her private means. She lived in respectable seclusion; she was of a soft but fairly cheerful disposition. She had been about eighteen at the time of her husband's death; she had been married only a year and had just borne him a son. From the day of his death she had devoted herself heart and soul to bringing up her precious treasure, her boy Kolya. Though she had loved him passionately those fourteen years, he had caused her far more suffering than happiness. She had been trembling and fainting with terror almost every day, afraid he would fall ill, catch cold, get up to some mischief, climb on a chair and fall off it, and so on and so on. When Kolya started going to school, the mother devoted herself to studying all the subjects with him so she could help him and go through his lessons at his side. She hurried to make the acquaintance of his teachers and their wives; she even sucked up to Kolya's schoolmates and flattered them in hopes of sparing Kolya from being teased, laughed at, or beaten by them. She went so far that the boys actually began mocking him because of her, taunting him with being a “mother's darling.”

But the boy could stand up for himself. He was a resolute boy, “tremendously strong,” as the rumor went in his class, and that soon proved to be true; he was agile, strong-willed, and of an audacious and enterprising temperament. He was good at his lessons, and there was a rumor at the school that he could beat the teacher, Dardanelov, at arithmetic and universal history. Though he looked down on everyone, he was a good comrade and not supercilious. He accepted his schoolmates' respect as his due, but he was friendly with them. Above all, he knew where to draw the line. He could restrain himself when necessary, and in his dealings with the teachers he never crossed that final, mysterious limit beyond which a prank becomes an unpardonable breach of discipline. But he was as fond of mischief at every opportunity as the smallest boy in the school—not so much for the mischief itself, but for the sake of creating a sensation, inventing something striking and conspicuous. He was extremely vain. He knew how to make even his mother give way to him; he was almost despotic in his control over her. She gave way to him—oh, she had been giving way to him for years. The one thing she could not bear was the thought that her boy didn't really love her. She was always imagining that Kolya was “unfeeling” toward her, and at times, dissolving into hysterical tears, she would reproach him for his coldness. The boy disliked this, and the more demonstrations of feeling were demanded of him, the more he seemed deliberately to avoid them. Yet it wasn't deliberate on his part but instinctive—it was his character. His mother was mistaken; he was very fond of her. He only disliked “sheepish sentimentality,” as he put it in his schoolboy language.

There was a bookcase in the house containing a few books that had belonged to his father. Kolya liked to read and had worked his way through several of them on his own. His mother didn't mind and was only occasionally surprised to see the boy stand for hours by the bookcase, poring over a book instead of going out to play. And in this way Kolya read some things unsuitable for his age.

Though the boy, as a rule, knew where to draw the line in his mischief, he had lately begun to play pranks that seriously alarmed his mother. It's true there was nothing vicious in what he did, but there was a wild, mad recklessness.

It happened that July, during the summer holidays, that the mother and son went to another district, forty-five miles away, to spend a week with a distant relation whose husband was an official at the railway station (the very station, the one nearest our town, from which a month later Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov set off for Moscow). There Kolya began by carefully investigating every detail connected with the railways, knowing he could impress his schoolmates back home with his newly acquired knowledge. But there happened to be some other boys in the area with whom he soon made friends. Some of them were living at the station, others nearby; there were six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, and two of them came from our town. The boys played together, and on the fourth or fifth day of Kolya's stay at the station, a mad bet was struck between these foolish boys. Kolya, who was almost the youngest of the group and consequently rather looked down on by the others, was moved by vanity or reckless bravado to bet them two roubles that he would lie down between the rails at night when the eleven o'clock train was due, and would lie there without moving while the train rolled over him at full speed. True, they conducted a preliminary investigation, which showed that it was possible to lie flat enough between the rails for the train to pass over without touching you—but to actually lie there was no joke! Kolya insisted stoutly that he would. At first they laughed at him, called him a little liar, a braggart—but that only egged him on. What galled him most was that these fifteen-year-old boys turned up their noses at him with too much superiority, and were at first inclined to treat him as “a small boy,” not fit to associate with them—and that was an unendurable insult.

So it was resolved that they would go out in the evening, half a mile from the station, so the train would have time to pick up full speed after leaving the station. The boys gathered. It was a pitch-dark night without a moon. At the appointed time, Kolya lay down between the rails. The five others who had taken the bet waited in the bushes below the embankment, their hearts pounding with suspense, which turned into alarm and remorse. At last they heard in the distance the rumble of the train leaving the station. Two red lights gleamed out of the darkness; the monster roared as it approached.

“Run, run away from the rails,” the boys cried to Kolya from the bushes, breathless with terror. But it was too late: the train darted up and flew past. The boys rushed to Kolya. He lay without moving. They began pulling at him, lifting him up. He suddenly got to his feet and walked away without a word. Then he explained that he had lain there as though unconscious in order to frighten them, but the truth was that he really had lost consciousness, as he confessed long afterwards to his mother. In this way his reputation as “a desperate character” was established forever. He returned to the house at the station as white as a sheet. The next day he had a slight attack of nervous fever, but he was in high spirits and very pleased with himself. The incident didn't become known at once, but once they got back to town it penetrated the school and even reached the ears of the masters. Then Kolya's mother hurried to plead with the masters on her boy's behalf, and in the end Dardanelov, a respected and influential teacher, intervened on his side, and the affair was dropped.

Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor who had been passionately in love with Madame Krassotkin for many years, and once already, about a year earlier, he had ventured—trembling with fear and the delicacy of his feelings—to offer her, most respectfully, his hand in marriage. But she had refused him flatly, feeling that to accept him would be an act of betrayal toward her son—though Dardanelov had, judging by certain mysterious symptoms, some reason to believe he was not an object of aversion to the charming but too chaste and tender-hearted widow. Kolya's mad prank seemed to have broken the ice, and Dardanelov was rewarded for his intercession with a suggestion of hope. The suggestion, it's true, was a faint one, but then Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that for the moment it was enough to make him perfectly happy. He was fond of the boy, though he would have thought it beneath him to try to win him over, and he was severe and strict with him in class. Kolya, too, kept him at a respectful distance. He learned his lessons perfectly; he was second in his class, was reserved with Dardanelov, and the whole class firmly believed that Kolya was so good at universal history that he could “beat” even Dardanelov. Kolya had indeed once asked him the question, “Who founded Troy?” to which Dardanelov had given a very vague reply, referring to the movements and migrations of races, the remoteness of the period, the mythical legends. But the question of who had founded Troy—that is, what individuals—he could not answer, and for some reason even regarded the question as idle and frivolous. But the boys remained convinced that Dardanelov did not know who founded Troy. Kolya had read of the founders of Troy in Smaragdov, whose history was among the books in his father's bookcase. In the end all the boys became interested in the question of who had founded Troy, but Krassotkin wouldn't give up his secret, and his reputation for knowledge remained intact.

After the incident on the railway a certain change came over Kolya's attitude toward his mother. When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) heard of her son's exploit, she almost went out of her mind with horror. She had such terrible attacks of hysterics, lasting on and off for several days, that Kolya, seriously alarmed at last, promised on his honor that such pranks would never be repeated. He swore on his knees before the holy image, and swore by the memory of his father, at Madame Krassotkin's urging—and the “manly” Kolya burst into tears like a boy of six. And all that day mother and son kept rushing into each other's arms, sobbing. The next day Kolya woke up as “unfeeling” as before, but he had become more silent, more modest, sterner, more thoughtful.

Six weeks later, it's true, he got into another scrape, one that even brought his name to the ears of our Justice of the Peace—but it was a scrape of quite a different sort, amusing, silly, and as it turned out he had not played the leading part in it, but was only implicated in it. But more on that later. His mother still fretted and trembled, but the more uneasy she became, the greater grew Dardanelov's hopes. It should be noted that Kolya understood and guessed what was in Dardanelov's heart, and of course despised him profoundly for his “feelings.” In the past he had been so tactless as to show this contempt in front of his mother, hinting vaguely that he knew what Dardanelov was after. But after the railway incident his behavior on this score changed too; he never allowed himself the slightest allusion to the subject and began to speak more respectfully of Dardanelov in front of his mother—which the sensitive woman at once appreciated with boundless gratitude. But at the faintest mention of Dardanelov by a visitor in Kolya's presence, she would flush as pink as a rose. At such moments Kolya would either stare out of the window scowling, or study the state of his boots, or shout angrily for “Perezvon”—the big, shaggy, mangy dog he had picked up a month before, brought home, and for some reason kept secretly indoors, not showing him to any of his schoolmates. He bullied him frightfully, teaching him all sorts of tricks, so that the poor dog howled for him whenever he was off at school, and when he came in, would whine with delight, rush about like a crazy thing, beg, lie down on the ground pretending to be dead, and so on—in fact, go through all the tricks Kolya had taught him, not at the word of command but simply out of the zeal of his excited and grateful heart.

I have forgotten, by the way, to mention that Kolya Krassotkin was the boy stabbed with a penknife by the boy already known to the reader as the son of Captain Snegiryov. Ilusha had been defending his father when the schoolboys jeered at him, shouting the nickname “wisp of tow.”
